messages.subject: Alpha attribute---
parts:
Good morning, All

I am a new ggplot2 user and currently just finished chapter 4 of Hadley's "ggplot2" book. Excuse my silly question beforehand. 

I am working with propensity scores. I created a data set with matched vs. unmatched groups. As Hadley expressed in the book, I wanted to explore this relationships visually on some continuous variables. I wrote the following code to display a density plot, which actually produce a plot I viewed in the book. However, my advisor suggested that I reduces the transparency so the difference could be seen more visually. Hadley mentions use of the alpha function to lower the transparency but when I include that feature I receive an error. Believe me, I am in my infancy with R and surely know I am doing something silly. If any one would be so kind to look at my code and offer any solutions would be greatly appreciated. In closing, not sure of the group culture but I was attempting to be clear and hope this was not too long of a description. 

Thank you all. 

Code: 
ggplot(testframe, aes(age, fill = label, alpha = I(1/5))) + geom_density (pos="dodge")

Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type AsIs. Defaulting to continuous
Error in data.frame(x = c(66L, 79L, 50L, 52L, 55L, 50L, 58L, 28L, 83L,  : 
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 3818, 1

Thanks again.

messages.author: 27405c4b711a1080
messages.subject: Re: Alpha attribute---
parts:
If you want to reduce the alpha of everything the same, you should put it outside of aes() and into the geom_(). I've never used I() successfully and haven't had the time to really its usage. 

library(ggplot2)
testframe <- data.frame(label = rep(c("matched", "unmatched"), 1000), age = rnorm(1000, 50, 25))
ggplot(testframe, aes(age, fill = label)) + geom_density (alpha = 0.2, pos="dodge")

HTH,

Brandon

messages.author: 27405c4b711a1080
messages.subject: Re: Alpha attribute---
parts:
Calls within aes() are mapped to variables. This is what's happening with your fill variable. You have a factor (label) that has two levels (matched and unmatched). These variables are mapped to blue and pink and displayed.

You can supply a single value to the alpha in either the geom_() or aes() and you get the same result. (I thought I previously tried in aes() and failed, but my history says otherwise). 
ggplot(testframe, aes(age, fill = label, alpha = 0.2)) + geom_density (pos="dodge")
ggplot(testframe, aes(age, fill = label)) + geom_density (alpha = 0.2, pos="dodge")

When you add I() to the mix, I'm not actually sure what it's doing. According to ?I():

Function I has two main uses.
  • In function data.frame. Protecting an object by enclosing it in I() in a call to data.frame inhibits the conversion of character vectors to factors and the dropping of names, and ensures that matrices are inserted as single columns. I can also be used to protect objects which are to be added to a data frame, or converted to a data frame via as.data.frame.
    • It achieves this by prepending the class "AsIs" to the object's classes. Class "AsIs" has a few of its own methods, including for [, as.data.frame, print and format.
  • In function formula. There it is used to inhibit the interpretation of operators such as "+", "-", "*" and "^" as formula operators, so they are used as arithmetical operators. This is interpreted as a symbol by terms.formula.
The error it gives is as though it is only trying to change the alpha of a single row in your data.frame. This obviously wouldn't work, but if you make it long enough it does.
Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type AsIs. Defaulting to continuous

Error in data.frame(x = c(82.4619328011436, 75.1021362110384, 41.8425680146036, : arguments imply differing number of rows: 2000, 1

ggplot(testframe, aes(age, fill = label, alpha = I(rep(0.2, 2000)))) + geom_density (pos="dodge")
Don't know how to automatically pick scale for object of type AsIs. Defaulting to continuous

I'm sorry if this isn't terribly satisfying. Perhaps someone else that knows more could round out both of our understanding. 

Brandon

On Fri, Jan 9, 2015 at 9:09 AM, Dottington Fullwood <dotco...@gmail.com> wrote:
Good morning, Brandon

Thank you so much for this guidance. 

To make sure I fully grasp this concept. By placing the alpha in the geom layer, that informs ggplot to apply the alpha to that particular layer as opposed to my earlier behavior of placing the alpha with in the context of building block of the plot to be displayed. 

Thanks again. I truly appreciate your time and rapid response. 

Happy New Year.

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Alpha attribute---
parts:
I'm responding to Brandon's post but the message is actually directed at the OP.

In ggplot2, I() is used to set the value of an aesthetic in qplot(). The idiom does not extend to ggplot() AFAIK. This is one reason why (IMO), when learning ggplot2,
one should stick to either qplot() or ggplot() while learning the package. Once the principles are understood, it's easier to jump back and forth between them without being confused by their syntactic differences. I tend to use ggplot() almost exclusively, but that's my choice - many people use both interchangeably with great success.

If you map an aesthetic to a single value inside aes(), it will produce a legend with that single value rendered. ggplot2 renders legends for aesthetics that are mapped - either to variables (preferred) or single values (usually unwanted, but not always). [There are a couple of exceptions to the rule about mapped variables automatically producing legends, but they are not relevant to your present example.]

Another feature worth knowing is that aesthetics mapped in ggplot() via aes() are passed down to all layers (produced by geoms or stats) that "understand" those aesthetics. (See the help page of a geom/stat to learn which aesthetics it understands.) Sometimes this feature is undesirable, in which case you want to perform aesthetic mappings within a geom or stat call.

Finally, it's easier to provide help if you supply a minimal reproducible example, or at the very least, a data frame (preferably in dput() form) plus the code you tried that triggered the error along with some reasonable description of what you want. Google "reproducible answer R" and you will be directed to several pages that well describe how to formulate a question in an R-help related group (including this one) that will maximize the probability of a positive outcome.

Dennis
